column3: It repeats the focus formula exactly, preserving the exception for Allah's purified servants.
Following unbelief and desire toward ruin loosely contrasts with the focus's protected servants.
Exclusive worship of Allah is joined to warning of painful punishment, matching both sides of the focus's contrast.
It repeats the focus formula exactly in the later polemic against false claims about Allah.
It immediately identifies the excepted servants as recipients of their appointed provision.
Satan's claimed reach explicitly excludes Allah's purified servants.
It repeats the focus formula exactly as an exception from the fate of earlier peoples.
The speech of a saved companion belongs to the ensuing scene of the excepted servants' security.
Allah's special selection of the patriarchs through purified remembrance supports the focus's purified-servant identity.
It uses the exact phrase Allah's purified servants in a declaration of the devotion people claimed they would have shown.
The display of Moses' hand has no material link to purified servitude or the exception from punishment.
It directly commands making religion exclusively Allah's, the core sense of purified devotion.
It explicitly exempts Allah's purified servants from Satan's misleading reach.
It continues the immediate description of the honoured provision granted to the excepted servants.
The speakers describe themselves as sincere exclusively to Allah while distinguishing their deeds from others'.
Allah's servants are invoked against Pharaoh's domination, but the verse does not concern their purification or exemption.
The saved speaker says a companion nearly brought about his ruin, clarifying the peril escaped in the reward scene.
The consecrated she-camel is unrelated to Allah's purified servants or their exception.
The exception for steadfast worshippers offers a broad formal parallel to the focus's exception.
Choosing Allah and the Hereafter over worldly life is rewarded, supporting the focus's devoted and favoured group.
It commands believing servants to worship Allah alone, directly supporting exclusive divine servitude.
Seeking only the face of the highest Lord expresses undivided intention akin to purified devotion.
It continues the immediate account of the excepted servants' place in gardens of bliss.
Striving for Allah and receiving guidance supports devotion generally but does not identify the purified exception.
The messengers' duty of clear delivery does not bear on purified servants or exemption from punishment.
It continues the reward scene by describing the drink of the excepted servants as free of harm.
It explicitly declares worship and religion as exclusively for Allah.
It states that Satan has no authority over Allah's servants except willing followers, closely explaining protected servitude.
The warning against religious excess and following desires lacks a specific link to the focus's exception.
Dire danger strips away rivals and produces a direct appeal with religion made exclusively for Allah.
Allah's servants are portrayed enjoying and distributing a heavenly spring, resonating with the focus's rewarded servants.
It continues the immediate depiction of the excepted servants seated facing one another.
The command requires worshipping Allah with religion made exclusively His.
Joseph is explicitly named among Allah's purified servants and is turned away from evil and indecency.
It is the saved servants' declaration that their deliverance and reward constitute the great triumph.
Creation for worship establishes the basic Allah-servant relation underlying the focus.
The sea crisis exposes religion made exclusively for Allah and its later reversal into association.
The distinction between believers who do good and evildoers only broadly echoes the focus's separation.
The claim of an exclusively reserved Hereafter offers a lexical but not substantive parallel to purified servitude.
It commands calling upon the one living God with religion made exclusively His.
It continues the immediate service of a flowing cup to the excepted servants.
Withdrawal from false worship leads to Allah's mercy, giving a concrete form to exclusive devotion and separation.
It explicitly defines the command as worshipping Allah with religion made exclusively His.
It continues the immediate description of the servants' pleasurable heavenly drink.
Allah's provision for His servants is a general servant relation without the focus's purification or exception.
Overwhelming danger makes people call on Allah with religion purified exclusively for Him.
Repentance, holding fast to Allah, and making religion exclusively His move people into the believing community and reward.
It begins the contrasting address to the idolaters and what they worship, from which the purified-servant exception follows.
The true revealed Book is followed by the direct command to worship Allah with religion exclusively His.
It continues the immediate heavenly scene of the excepted servants.
It denies that alleged objects of worship knowingly received that worship, reinforcing the rejection of divided devotion.
Avoiding false powers and turning back to Allah brings glad tidings to His servants.
The invitation to look continues the saved companions' observation of the condemned companion in the reward scene.
Acknowledging Allah's ownership is pressed toward God-conscious response, supporting exclusive allegiance.
It exposes supposed deities as servants like their callers, undermining worship directed away from Allah.
The final reward of truthful people in gardens supports the outcome assigned to the focus's purified servants.
Calling Zechariah Allah's servant is a generic servant designation without the focus's exception.
It counters the claim that the Merciful has a child by calling the beings honoured servants, relevant to true divine relation.
It continues the immediate description of the excepted servants' heavenly companions.
Moses is explicitly described as purified and as Allah's messenger and prophet.
It states that pure religion belongs to Allah and rejects mediation through other protectors.
The saved companion's view of another in Hell clarifies the punitive fate from which his company was spared.
It shows that admitting Allah's ownership should become remembrance and responsive allegiance.
Allah's chosen religion and the command to die in submission support exclusive, enduring devotion.
The God-conscious are placed in gardens and springs, closely paralleling the focus's rewarded exception.
Allah's distinctive mark is paired with the declaration that we worship Him.
The parable's differing reception and the description of transgressors do not specifically address purified servitude.
Allah's knowledge of hidden and visible deeds has no specific connection to the focus's exception.
Allah's creation of people and their acts affirms divine mastery but not purified-servant separation.
The verse reserves provision exclusively for believers on the Day of Resurrection, echoing the focus's privileged outcome.
The number of later recipients in a heavenly ranking has only a distant relation to the focus's reward scene.
It joins upright worship with calling upon Allah while making religion exclusively His and returning to Him.
The test distinguishing faithful followers from those who turn back only generally resembles a separating judgment.
The staff's transformation has no meaningful link to purified servants or exclusive devotion.
Hud commands his people to worship Allah alone and be God-conscious.
The disputed claim of limited fire punishment only loosely relates to the focus's contrast of punishment and exception.
The God-conscious are placed in gardens and springs, paralleling the reward assigned to the excepted servants.
Joseph's selection for royal service is not the religious purification or divine exception expressed in the focus.
The detailed nursing and support regulations do not bear on the focus's servant or punishment theme.
It combines worship of Allah with fearing Him, supporting the exclusive devotion of Allah's servants.
The coming judgment and return of all matters to Allah loosely frame the accountability behind the exception.
The denial of the false claim that Allah fathered a child belongs to the same surah's correction of false speech about Him.
The history of revelation, disagreement, and guidance does not specifically link to purified servants.
Provision for servants and resurrection supply a broad background of divine care and final outcome.
The statement about self-deception by hypocrites has no specific connection to the focus.
The Prophet is called Allah's servant, but the verse does not concern purified devotion or exemption.
The punishment of those who bar Allah's remembrance has only a general contrast with the saved servants.
A servant granted mercy and knowledge illustrates dependent servitude but not the focus's purified exception.
The Prophet's specific marital permissions do not materially relate to purified servants or exclusive devotion.
Gratitude for Allah's provision is tied to worshipping Him, but remains a general devotional instruction.
The call to fear Allah and obey His messenger supports obedience generally without the focus's purification theme.
It commands worship of the one Lord shared by Jesus and his hearers, supporting exclusive divine servitude.
It sharply contrasts those pursuing Allah's pleasure with those returning under wrath and Hell.
Calling Allah the God of people establishes His lordship but not the focus's purified-servant exception.
The extension of the hypocrites in transgression has no material link to the focus.
It directly commands prostration and worship of Allah alone.
A people loved by Allah and devoted to His cause offers a broad portrait of faithful allegiance.
Satan's claim to take an appointed share of Allah's servants contrasts with the focus's servants who are excluded from ruin.
The signs and dispute described here do not specifically concern purified servants or their exception.
Jesus is defined as a servant favoured by Allah, countering any elevation that compromises divine-exclusive servitude.
It identifies the Day of Judgment whose punishment sequence the focus immediately qualifies by exception.
It names the Day of Decision, the judgment setting for the condemned group excluded from the focus's purified servants.
It orders the gathering of wrongdoers, their associates, and their objects of worship before the focus separates another group.
It directs the gathered wrongdoers toward Hell, establishing the destination from which the focus's exception stands apart.
It halts the condemned for questioning, supplying the accountability that precedes the exception in the focus.
Its question about mutual help exposes the powerlessness of the condemned collective contrasted with the protected servants.
It describes the condemned as submitting on that Day, the opposite outcome to the honoured exception at the focus.
The condemned turn to question one another, continuing the culpability sequence immediately before the focus.
The followers blame their leaders, specifying the divided allegiance that leads into the shared punishment.
The leaders deny compulsion and call the followers transgressors, assigning responsibility within the condemned group.
It denies that the leaders held authority over the followers, clarifying culpability before the focus's exception.
It confirms that the Lord's word of punishment has become binding on the condemned and will be tasted.
The leaders admit leading others astray while already astray themselves, completing the causal account of the punishment.
It states that both parties will share the punishment, the collective fate from which the focus excepts Allah's purified servants.
It generalizes the preceding treatment as Allah's dealing with the guilty, directly framing the focus's exception.
It identifies the guilty response as arrogance when told that there is no god but Allah.
It records their refusal to abandon their gods, the divided worship opposite to purified devotion to Allah.
It affirms that the messenger brought truth and confirmed the messengers, answering the rejection that precedes the focus.
It announces the painful punishment that the focus immediately excludes for Allah's purified servants.
It states that recompense follows what the condemned used to do, immediately before the exception in 37:40.
It calls all parties to worship none but Allah and to take no lords besides Him, directly expressing undivided devotion.
It commands worship of Allah and association of nothing with Him, the clearest opposite of divided worship.
It condemns deifying the Messiah and affirms worship of Allah alone, with Paradise tied to avoiding association.
It rejects the attribution of worship to Jesus and his mother and reasserts worship due to Allah alone.
It identifies Allah as the sole Creator and commands worship of Him, directly grounding exclusive servitude.
It dedicates prayer, sacrifice, life, and death wholly to Allah, a comprehensive statement of purified devotion.
It denies any partner to Allah and frames submission as the speaker's defining allegiance.
It condemns taking religious authorities as lords while affirming the command to worship the one God.
It commands worship of Allah alone and rejects worship of anything others worship besides Him.
It declares that judgment belongs only to Allah and commands worship of none but Him.
It states that the messenger is commanded to worship Allah and not associate anything with Him.
Satan vows to lure humanity through embellishment, supplying the threat from which the purified servants are exempted in the next verse.
It commands continuing worship of the Lord until certainty arrives, sustaining the single Lord-servant relation.
It gives the recurring prophetic command: worship Allah and avoid false powers.
It denies Satan authority over those who believe and rely on their Lord, closely paralleling protected servants.
Allah declares that Satan has no authority over His servants, a direct companion to the purified-servant exception.
It requires righteous action without associating anyone in worship of the Lord.
Allah declares His sole divinity and commands worship of Him with prayer for His remembrance.
Every messenger is sent with the declaration that there is no god but Allah and that He alone must be worshipped.
Noah commands his people to worship Allah, affirming that they have no god other than Him.
A later messenger gives the same command to worship Allah alone, reinforcing the exclusive-devotion pattern.
The faithful servants do not call upon another god with Allah, directly excluding divided worship.
It prohibits calling upon another god with Allah and affirms that all judgment returns to Him.
Satan has no authority over people except as a test, clarifying that his influence does not override divine servitude.
Satan vows to mislead all, setting up the explicit exception for Allah's purified servants in the following verse.
It rejects any command to worship other than Allah after the preceding declarations of pure religion.
It commands worship of Allah alone and gratitude to Him, resolving the rejection of all other worship.
It forbids worship of those called besides Allah and commands submission to the Lord of the worlds.
It commands worship of Allah alone rather than the sun or moon, explicitly excluding rival objects of worship.
It declares Allah the shared Lord and commands worship of Him as the straight path.
It commands fleeing to Allah and forbids setting another god alongside Him.
It declares that places of worship belong to Allah and forbids calling upon anyone with Him.
It states that the messenger calls only upon his Lord and associates no one with Him.
